newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INSTANT VIEW-Australian balance on goods/services.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW-Australian balance on goods/services.

text.p: Australia's balance on international trade in goods and services posted a deficit of A$103 million in March, official figures showed.
Economists' median forecasts had centred on a surplus of A$150 million, with forecasts ranging from a A$150 million deficit to a A$550 million surplus.
In February, the balance was was a surplus of A$315 million.
A selection of economists' immediate reactions to the data follows.
DAVID DE GARIS, SENIOR TREASURY ECONOMIST, ANZ BANK:

"I think with the volatility in these monthly numbers, you have to be a little bit careful of reading too much into one month. We thought that non-rural exports were particularly strong the past couple of months and were due for a correction this month. I think on the basis of these numbers we're still looking at a current account deficit of probably less than A$5 billion in the March quarter. That's still a lot lower than the deficits that we had through most of last year."
BRUCE FREELAND, CHIEF ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK OF AUSTRALIA:

"The fact that it was in deficit was a surprise. The reason why it wasn't in line with our expectations was that we were expecting a lesser fall in exports than actually occurred. The fall in imports was pretty much as expected. But, by and large, it's still very much a number which should be neutral for markets and still showing Australia, in an overall sense, basically hovering around a balance on goods and services. That, I think, will continue to be the story."
MATTHEW DRENNAN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, AXIOM FUNDS MANAGEMENT:

"There is certainly a lot of monthly volatility in these figures, but I think if you look at quarterly perspective, what we've got now is only a net improvement of about A$200 million over what we had in the December quarter, which means that we could very well end up with a current account deficit of A$5 billion or greater in the March quarter. So that's not a great trend and it's pretty much in line with what we were expecting at Axiom, that we are going to see some deterioration in the current account deficit as we move through into 1997/98."

"It's disappointing that exports have fallen away so much after showing some very encouraging signs of picking up through the course of the last six months or so. The falls have been pretty much across the board. There's not a one-off explanation that we can see for the deterioration. But it's not terribly bad because the monthly figures are highly volatile. If you put a trend line through it, we are still running four monthly surpluses on goods and services. But the trade account is looking OK."
STEPHEN ROBERTS, CHIEF ECONOMIST UBS AUSTRALIA

"They are quite consistent with everything else we have seen in the last month or so. It's just a touch of softness on the exports side, and also the imports side in March, although the previous two months have been a fair bit stronger. These are not really the crictcal numbers, but it was important that the import side came back as it did. It's another one of these indications that there has been a little bit of a pull back in the growth story running through the March quarter."
